Choosing and checking precision

Decide where to widen

Convert existing inputs before a numerically sensitive calculation. If the input is decimal text, read it directly into the chosen type. Higher-precision arithmetic can reduce rounding during the calculation. Any rounding in the original inputs is already part of the problem you are solving.

Keep values at the working precision through subsequent sensitive steps. Convert back to Float64 at an interface that needs it, such as a storage format or downstream routine. For a large workload, measure the accuracy and cost of widening the part where it makes a difference.

Measure the error you care about

Absolute error is the magnitude of the difference from a reference result. Relative error measures that distance as a fraction of the reference magnitude. Use an absolute tolerance near an expected zero, and a relative tolerance when the scale of a nonzero answer matters. For a linear system, a small residual A*x - b shows that the computed solution nearly satisfies the equations. How close it is to the desired solution also depends on the problem’s conditioning, meaning its sensitivity to changes in the data.

For two same-type DoubleFloats, scalar isapprox derives its default relative tolerance from the high components. It also accepts identical high components and uses an absolute floor of 1e-32. To validate the low component or apply a tighter absolute tolerance, measure the difference directly, as in the example below.

Keep a small correction

Here the quantity of interest is log(1 + δ). At this scale Float64 rounds 1 + δ to one. log1p computes the quantity directly, and a higher-precision reference lets us check the resulting error. The reference starts from the same decimal text as the working value. Comparing the two input representations at high precision isolates input rounding. The relative error of the final result includes both input rounding and arithmetic error.

using DoubleFloats

text = "1e-20"
δ = Double64(text)
result = log1p(δ)

input_errors, relative_error = setprecision(BigFloat, 256) do
    exact_input = parse(BigFloat, text)
    reference = log1p(exact_input)
    input_errors = abs.((BigFloat(parse(Float64, text)) - exact_input,
                         BigFloat(δ) - exact_input))
    input_errors, abs(BigFloat(result) - reference) / abs(reference)
end

@assert log(1 + parse(Float64, text)) == 0.0
@assert input_errors[2] < input_errors[1]
@assert relative_error < big"1e-29"
println("Relative error: ", Float64(relative_error))
Relative error: 1.3959760021627682e-33

The Accuracy Report gives sampled errors and matrix residuals for a range of functions. The input ranges and metrics matter when comparing those results with your computation.
